name: Vector Search Inside SQL Databases
title: Vector Search Inside SQL Databases
answer: Vector search stores embeddings, lists of numbers that represent meaning, and finds the nearest ones to a query. Extensions such as pgvector let a relational database do this alongside normal tables, so retrieval can respect the same joins, filters and permissions as the rest of the data. This puts semantic retrieval inside the database rather than in a separate service. The result is that a query can combine meaning-based similarity with ordinary SQL conditions in one place.

Extensions such as pgvector let a relational database do this alongside normal tables, so retrieval can respect the same joins, filters and permissions as the rest of the data. sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: Vector search inside SQL databases runs as an extension or native feature of the database engine itself. In PostgreSQL, pgvector adds a vector column type and index types for approximate nearest neighbor search. The work happens on the same server, storage and backup systems that already hold the relational data. For larger deployments, the vector index may sit in memory or on fast local storage, and the database may be tuned for the extra memory and compute that similarity search requires.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Embeddings are generated by a model, stored in a vector column, and queried by comparing the query embedding to stored vectors using a distance measure such as cosine or Euclidean distance. To make this fast, the database builds an approximate nearest neighbor index, often HNSW or IVFFlat, which trades a small amount of recall for speed. Queries can combine vector similarity with standard SQL filters, joins and ordering, so a single statement can retrieve rows that are both semantically close and meet business conditions. Hybrid search, mixing vector scores with keyword scores, is common when exact terms matter.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Because vectors live in the same database, existing access controls, row-level security and audit logs can apply to them. Embeddings can leak information about the text they represent, so many teams treat them as sensitive data. Provenance matters: teams often track which model produced an embedding, when, and from what source, because a model change can invalidate old vectors. Retention and deletion rules often cover vector columns as well as the original content, and if embeddings are derived from personal data, privacy rules may apply.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The line between vector databases and relational databases continues to blur, with more SQL engines adding native vector types and indexes. Agent frameworks and Model Context Protocol servers are making it easier for AI systems to query these databases directly, and the site currently tracks 263 MCP servers for SQL databases and warehouses. Expect tighter integration of embedding generation inside the database, better hybrid query planners, and more standard ways to manage embedding versions and permissions. The goal is to let teams use one system for both structured and semantic retrieval without copying data into a separate store.
